questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: A Behaviour That Needs No Practice
questions.learningObjective: separate a species-typical behaviour from one that depends on experience
questions.stem: Newborn lambs stagger to their feet and stay close to their mothers within minutes, with no rehearsal at all. Which account best explains that?

options.text: The behaviour is species-typical, so it appears without practice because the machinery is already in place
The behaviour was learnt in utero, so no rehearsal is needed once the lamb has been born
options.misconception: assumes prenatal rehearsal produced a whole motor programme

options.text: The behaviour is a conditioned reflex built up over the first hours of life with the mother as the signal
options.misconception: reads a species-typical action as a conditioned response

options.text: The behaviour depends on having seen the mother walk, so it counts as learning by watching a model
options.misconception: assumes a newborn can imitate a model it has barely seen

questions.explanation: The useful contrast here is between a behaviour that needs no history and one that does, and the test of which is which is simple: does it appear without the organism ever having encountered the situation? A lamb that stands and follows within minutes of birth has no such history, so the machinery for standing and following has to be present already, which is what species-typical means. The prenatal-rehearsal option fails because learning a motor programme before birth would still require a rehearsal schedule, and no such history is available for a behaviour performed in the first minutes of life. The conditioned-reflex option fails because a conditioned response needs pairings of two events, and there has been no pairing here. The imitation option fails because a newborn is not in a position to copy a model, and following the mother is a response to her presence rather than a reproduction of a movement.
questions.hint: Ask whether the behaviour could be performed by an organism that had never met the situation before.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: What the First Pairing Produces
questions.learningObjective: state that conditioning builds an association between a signal and a trigger
questions.stem: A tone is played forty times with nothing else happening and a dog shows nothing to it. The tone is then played forty times with food, after which the dog's ear turns at the sound. What has the second set of pairings built?

options.text: An association between the tone and the food, so the tone alone can now bring the response about
A reflex the dog was born with, which the food has merely made visible for the first time
options.misconception: reads a learned association as an inborn unconditioned reflex

options.text: A muscle response made firmer by repetition, whatever the tone happens to predict
options.misconception: treats conditioning as nothing but physical practice of a movement

options.text: A habit formed by repeating one act until it can be done without thinking about it
options.misconception: confuses a conditioned response with an automatic motor habit

questions.explanation: Before the food appeared, the tone was just a sound, and forty presentations of a sound produce nothing on their own, which is the control the experimenter has already run. Once the tone is repeatedly followed by food, the tone acquires a value it did not have, and the response to food can be triggered by the sound instead. That is the whole content of the learning: an association, so that a signal which predicts nothing in particular can come to call up a response. The inborn-reflex option fails because an unconditioned response is one that needs no learning, and a response to a novel sound is not that. The practice option fails because nothing was practised and nothing needed to be, and the response appeared to a signal rather than to a practised act. The habit option fails because a habit is a behaviour performed fluently, and what is described here is a response to a stimulus that predicts food.
questions.hint: Ask what the tone was worth before the food was paired with it, and what it is worth afterwards.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: Naming the Learned Part
questions.learningObjective: apply the conditioning terms to a described procedure
questions.stem: After many pairings, a dog salivates to a bell that is never again followed by food, and shows no reaction to a buzzer. Which label fits the salivating to the bell?

options.text: It is the conditioned response, since the bell has become the learned signal standing in for the food
It is the unconditioned response, because salivating to food is what the bell now brings about
options.misconception: keeps the original name for a signal the subject has learnt

options.text: It is the unconditioned stimulus, because the bell is the thing that sets the response off
options.misconception: uses the term for a trigger where the term for a response belongs

options.text: It is discrimination, since the dog withholds the response when the buzzer sounds instead
options.misconception: answers a naming question with a description of stimulus control

questions.explanation: The two words in the phrase are not interchangeable, and the test is whether the event needed the history. Salivating to food needs none, so that is the unconditioned response, and the bell is a sound that started out meaning nothing and now stands for the food, so it is the conditioned stimulus and the salivating to it is the conditioned response. The unconditioned-response option fails because it keeps the original name for a response that could not have occurred before the learning, and the label is defined by exactly that absence of history. The unconditioned-stimulus option fails because it names the bell as a trigger, but a trigger that was installed by pairing is precisely the thing the term conditioned stimulus exists to describe. The discrimination option fails because discrimination is a process, not a label for a response, and the withholding to the buzzer is evidence of it rather than the name of the salivating.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two events needed the pairing history, and which would have happened anyway.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: Building a Signal Out of a Signal
questions.learningObjective: identify second-order conditioning
questions.stem: A child is frightened by a man who is himself frightened by a book, and afterwards shows fear of books even when no man is in the room. What has happened?

options.text: Second-order conditioning, in which the book became a signal by being paired with the man's own fear
Second-order unconditioning, in which the book removed the fear the man had put into the scene
options.misconception: invents a conditioning term for the disappearance of a fear

options.text: Generalisation from the man's face to the shape of the book's cover, which resembled it
options.misconception: calls a newly learnt signal a perceptual blur of an old one

options.text: Extinction of the original fear, since the man no longer appears whenever the book is shown
options.misconception: claims a disappearing fear is what the pairing produced

questions.explanation: The telling detail is that the book had no history of its own, and the man's fear is not a reflex that a book could trigger by itself, so the book cannot have acquired its power directly. It acquired it by being present when something already frightening was present, which is the defining move of second-order conditioning: a signal that predicts nothing becomes a signal by being paired with a signal that already predicts something. The invented term fails because there is no such procedure, and the fear has spread rather than gone. The generalisation option fails because generalisation is the spread of a response from a trained stimulus to stimuli like it, and a book need not resemble a man for this to occur, so similarity is not what is doing the work. The extinction option fails because extinction requires the signal to be presented with nothing following it, and here the signal is presented in the company of a genuine threat.
questions.hint: Ask whether the book could ever have acquired its power on its own, and if not, what it was paired with.

questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: A Response That Spreads Across Similar Sounds
questions.learningObjective: name a stimulus generalisation gradient
questions.stem: A dog is conditioned to a 1200 Hz tone and then tested with tones from 400 to 2400 Hz, and it responds across a band centred on 1200 Hz. What is that band?

options.text: A stimulus generalisation gradient, since responding spreads outward from the tone that was trained
A discrimination, since the dog is now telling 1200 Hz tones apart from all the others
options.misconception: reads a spread of responding as an act of telling stimuli apart

options.text: An extinction, since the response is no longer confined to the one tone that was trained
options.misconception: treats any widening of responding as a loss of learning

options.text: A conditioned reflex, which is the name given to the width of the band a response covers
options.misconception: uses the term for a learnt link to name the width of a band

questions.explanation: A response that was installed by one tone does not stay politely confined to that one tone, and where it does spread is itself measurable, which is what makes the gradient a useful object of study rather than a nuisance. The gradient peaks at the trained value and falls away as the test tone moves further from it, and that shape is a direct measurement of how much the learned response depends on the exact signal. The discrimination option fails because discrimination is the opposite movement, the process by which a response is narrowed to one signal among several, and a band of responding is the picture before that narrowing has been trained. The extinction option fails because extinction needs many presentations of the signal with nothing following it, and the test tones here are being measured once each. The conditioned-reflex option fails because that phrase names the learned link between signal and response, not the range over which the response is expressed.
questions.hint: Ask whether the response has narrowed to one signal or spread away from it.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: Narrowing a Response to One Signal
questions.learningObjective: identify stimulus discrimination from a described contingency
questions.stem: A dog is conditioned to a red light, then receives a mild shock only when a blue light appears, and within a week salivates to red and not to blue. What has it learnt?

options.text: A discrimination between the two lights, so the response now depends on which of them is the signal
An extinction of the response to red, since red is no longer paired with anything at all
options.misconception: claims an old learning is erased when a new contingency is added

options.text: A generalisation from red to blue, since both lights look alike in a darkened room
options.misconception: reverses the terms for spreading a response and telling stimuli apart

options.text: A second-order conditioning of the blue light onto the red one, in one step of learning
options.misconception: borrows a two-stage conditioning term to name a single contingency

questions.explanation: Discrimination is trained by giving the organism a reason to respond differently to two stimuli, and here that reason has been supplied: the blue light has its own consequence and the red light keeps its own, so the two can be told apart in terms of what they lead to. The dog's salivating to red and withholding to blue is therefore the response coming under stimulus control, and the useful detail is that the blue light never produced food, so the withholding is not fear of it. The extinction option fails because extinction would require repeated presentations of red with nothing following, which is not what happened, and red still means food. The generalisation option fails because a spread of response and a narrowing of response are opposites, and the dog has narrowed rather than spread. The second-order option fails because a second-order sequence needs a new signal to be paired with an old one, and here no new signal has been made to stand for anything.
questions.hint: Ask what each light now predicts, and whether the dog responds the same way to both.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: The Response That Stops
questions.learningObjective: define extinction and state what it does and does not prove
questions.stem: A conditioned dog is played the tone alone twenty sessions running with no food, and its salivation falls to almost nothing. What is that fall called, and what does it show?

options.text: Extinction, showing the learned link is suppressed once the signal stops predicting the outcome
Extinction, showing the original learning has been permanently erased from the dog's memory
options.misconception: treats a fall in responding as proof the memory was destroyed

options.text: Spontaneous recovery, showing the response will return on its own without any fresh pairings
options.misconception: names a later return as though it were the fall being described

options.text: Unlearning, showing the dog has been returned to the unconditioned state it started in
options.misconception: claims that suppressing a response is the same as never having learnt

questions.explanation: Extinction is what happens when the signal keeps arriving and the outcome stops, and the reason the response declines is that the signal has quietly stopped being informative, so there is nothing left for the association to predict. The careful part of the claim is suppression rather than erasure, because the learning was demonstrated to be intact a moment ago and a mere rest or a single unreinforced presentation can undo the decline, which a destroyed memory could not do. The permanent-erasure option fails because it predicts that no amount of rest or retraining would bring the response back, and both do. The spontaneous-recovery option fails because that name belongs to a later return of the response after a rest, and nothing has been described as returning. The unlearning option fails because the dog was not in an unconditioned state to begin with, since it produced no salivation to the tone before the food appeared, so there is no earlier state to have been returned to.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the response if the animal is rested and the signal is presented once more.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: A Return After a Rest
questions.learningObjective: distinguish spontaneous recovery from reinstatement
questions.stem: A dog whose conditioned response has been extinguished is left alone for ten days, then played the tone once, and it salivates at once, though less strongly than before extinction. What is that?

options.text: Spontaneous recovery, in which the original learning reappears after a rest with no new pairing
Reinstatement, which would require the original food to be presented again before the tone
options.misconception: confuses a return after rest with a return caused by fresh pairings

options.text: Discrimination learning, since the dog responds to the tone and not to the buzzer
options.misconception: reads a recovery effect as an act of stimulus control

options.text: A fresh conditioning of the tone to the sound of the kennel during the ten days alone
options.misconception: invents a pairing to explain a return that needed none

questions.explanation: Nothing was paired with anything during the ten days, and the response is back anyway, so whatever produced the return was internal to the animal and had nothing to do with new information arriving. That is the signature of spontaneous recovery, and its importance is that it demonstrates the extinction effect was a suppression of the response rather than a destruction of the learning, because an intact association is exactly what can be recovered from. The reinstatement option fails because reinstatement is caused by presenting the original unconditioned stimulus, and no food was given, so the mechanism has not been engaged. The discrimination option fails because the dog is not being trained to withhold anything, and responding to the tone and not the buzzer was true before the rest as well. The fresh-conditioning option fails because it invents a pairing, and the defining feature of this effect is that the return occurs with nothing new presented at all.
questions.hint: Ask what was presented during the ten days, and whether anything new reached the dog.

questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: A Return Caused by Fresh Pairings
questions.learningObjective: identify reinstatement as distinct from spontaneous recovery
questions.stem: After a dog has stopped responding to a tone, the experimenter gives several presentations of food in a different room, and the next day the dog salivates to the tone again. What is at work?

options.text: Reinstatement, in which presenting the original trigger again restores responding to the signal
Spontaneous recovery, since the return follows a gap in which nothing was done to the dog
options.misconception: credits a rest for an effect that needed fresh pairings

options.text: Second-order conditioning, since the new room has taken over as the conditioned stimulus
options.misconception: reads an environmental cue as a whole second conditioning procedure

options.text: Reinforcement, since food was delivered and so the dog's salivation has been reinforced
options.misconception: treats the presentation of food as a consequence of the dog's own behaviour

questions.explanation: The food was presented without the tone anywhere in sight, and the tone was not present during any of those presentations, so what the food did was put the original association back in working order rather than teach the tone anything new. That is reinstatement, and the point of the term is that the animal's own responding to the signal had been extinguished, so the restoration is of a link that was already there and had gone quiet. The spontaneous-recovery option fails because that effect is precisely the one that needs nothing presented, and here something was. The second-order option fails because a new signal has not been made to stand for anything, and the room is a background cue rather than a signal carrying the food's meaning. The reinforcement option fails because reinforcement is a consequence that follows the animal's own act, and here the food was given out of the experimenter's schedule with no salivating to reward.
questions.hint: Ask whether the food was ever presented with the tone, and what that rules in and out.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: Taking Something Away and Strengthening a Behaviour
questions.learningObjective: identify negative reinforcement and separate it from punishment
questions.stem: A mother's unpleasant chores stop the moment a child's tantrum starts, and the tantrums grow steadily more frequent. What is doing the work?

options.text: Negative reinforcement of the tantrum, since removing something aversive strengthened the act that removed it
Positive punishment of the tantrum, since the mother is plainly doing something about the child's behaviour
options.misconception: treats any action taken over a child as punishment regardless of what follows

options.text: Negative punishment of the tantrum, since something the mother valued has been taken away from the child
options.misconception: confuses a removed aversive event with a removed valued one

options.text: Operant extinction of the tantrum, since once the chores are gone nothing at all follows the noise
options.misconception: calls a removal of an aversive event the same as withholding of consequence

questions.explanation: Two features do the identifying here. A consequence followed the tantrum, so extinction is ruled out, and that consequence strengthened the behaviour rather than suppressing it, so punishment is ruled out too. What makes it negative is that the consequence was the removal of something the child did not want, and what makes it reinforcing is that the behaviour which produced that removal has become more likely, which is precisely the pattern described. The positive-punishment option fails because the positive-negative pair describes what was added or removed, not how much the mother acted, and what was removed here was an unpleasant event. The negative-punishment option fails because punishment requires a valued stimulus to be taken away, and no such loss has occurred. The extinction option fails because extinction is the absence of any consequence, and here the disappearance of the chores is doing exactly the work of a consequence, arriving on the child's schedule rather than the mother's.
questions.hint: Ask what happened to the behaviour, then ask whether something was added or something was taken away.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: Separating the Consequence From the Thing Valued
questions.learningObjective: distinguish reinforcement from reward
questions.stem: A tutor tells a student that her written work is getting sharper, and her writing improves steadily over the following month. Which is the mechanism, and which is the reward?

options.text: Reinforcement, since the comment strengthened the work; the reward is the better mark that followed it
Reward, since the improved mark is what strengthened the writing over the whole month
options.misconception: treats the outcome the student valued as the consequence that taught

options.text: Both, since nothing else in her week could have produced a change lasting a month
options.misconception: declares two named processes interchangeable because both are present

options.text: Neither, since only outcomes with money or a grade attached can shape a behaviour at all
options.misconception: believes only material consequences can act on behaviour

questions.explanation: The two words sit on opposite sides of the behaviour, and keeping them apart is the whole point: reinforcement names the consequence and its effect on the behaviour, while reward names the thing that consequence delivered and that the person found worth having. A comment is a perfectly good reinforcer because what reinforcement requires is that the behaviour becomes more likely, and a student working harder for a month after being told her work has improved is exactly that, whatever the comment was worth in itself. The reversed option fails because it takes the valued outcome to be the teaching event, and the mark could not have caused the writing that earned it. The both option fails because one event cannot be two processes, and the description supplies a cause and an effect rather than a pair of labels. The neither option fails because nothing about the two words requires a material payoff, and informational consequences shape behaviour readily.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the behaviour each word sits on, and what happened to the writing afterwards.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: Why Bad Parking Persists After a Good Scare
questions.learningObjective: state that a consequence must be felt at the time to suppress a behaviour
questions.stem: A driver once felt the excitement of getting away with parking illegally, and years later still parks illegally. Which point about punishment does that support?

options.text: A consequence the person does not feel at the time of the act does little to suppress the act
A consequence works only when the rule-breaker receives it where others can see it happen
options.misconception: requires an audience before a consequence can change anything

options.text: A consequence works well only if it is severe enough to cause lasting physical discomfort
options.misconception: judges a consequence by how much physical hurt it produces

options.text: Illegal parking is one of the acts that no consequence has ever been able to change
options.misconception: concludes a behaviour is beyond the reach of consequences entirely

questions.explanation: Punishment works by adding or removing something so unpleasant that the behaviour stops being worth repeating, and that only happens if the unpleasantness arrives in the same moment as the act. Here the unpleasant arrival was long and uncertain, so it could not attach itself to the parking, while a small enjoyment did attach itself, and the balance that should have been tipped by the penalty was not. The audience option fails because nothing about a consequence's effect on the person receiving it depends on whether anyone else watches, and plenty of unobserved penalties work. The severity option fails because a consequence that lands with real but bearable force can suppress an act perfectly well, and the important variable is the felt pairing rather than the injury. The hopeless-behaviour option fails because it converts one stubborn case into a general claim, and plenty of drivers are deterred by an ordinary ticket.
questions.hint: Ask when the unpleasant consequence arrives relative to the act, and whether the act was ever followed by anything felt.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: A Rule About Number of Responses
questions.learningObjective: distinguish ratio schedules from interval schedules
questions.stem: One vending machine pays a snack only after five purchases, while another pays one every three minutes whether or not anything is bought. What is the first machine's rule, and what does it produce?

options.text: A fixed-ratio schedule, which ties the reward to a number of responses and so ties reward to effort
A variable-ratio schedule, which ties the reward to a number of responses that changes each time
options.misconception: uses the variable-ratio label for a requirement that never changes

options.text: A fixed-interval schedule, which ties the reward to a number of responses made within a time
options.misconception: reads a count of responses as though it were a passage of time

options.text: An extinction schedule, which ties the reward to nothing at all and so ends the buying
options.misconception: treats a rule about when to pay as though it were a rule against paying

questions.explanation: Schedules of reinforcement are named by two questions, and the first is whether the reward is tied to a number of responses or to elapsed time. Five purchases is a number of responses, so this is a ratio schedule, and the count never varies, so it is fixed. The useful consequence of tying reward to a count is that the reward becomes something the person produces rather than something that arrives, and the effort immediately before the fifth purchase is the effort that bought the snack. The variable-ratio option fails because a varying requirement is the other kind of ratio schedule, and nothing here varies. The fixed-interval option fails because three minutes is an example of the other kind of schedule altogether, and it ties reward to time rather than to a count of purchases. The extinction option fails because extinction means no consequence at all, and a machine that pays on the fifth purchase is precisely delivering a consequence.
questions.hint: Ask whether the reward waits for a number of acts or for a stretch of time.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: Which Schedule Holds a Response Steady
questions.learningObjective: predict response patterns under fixed and variable ratio schedules
questions.stem: One machine pays after exactly five purchases; another pays after a number of purchases that varies but averages five. Which holds a person's clicking steadier, and why?

options.text: The varying one, because a reward that might be one purchase away makes every first click worth making
The fixed one, because knowing the exact count makes the coming reward easier to anticipate
options.misconception: believes a guaranteed reward motivates more than an uncertain one

options.text: The varying one, because a count that changes each time can be worked out exactly in advance
options.misconception: credits the user with learning a rule that never repeats

options.text: Both equally, because the average number of purchases per reward is the same in each
options.misconception: treats a shared average as though it made the two rules identical

questions.explanation: The behaviour that a schedule produces is explained by what it does to the value of the next single response, and on a fixed count the fifth click is worth a great deal while the first is worth nothing, so the pattern breaks into bursts separated by pauses. On a varying count the first click of any set might be the one that pays, so no click can be safely skipped, and the steady high rate follows from that arithmetic rather than from the average. The fixed-one option fails because a certain reward after a certain count creates a pause to be passed through, and a predictable reward has no reason to be hurried. The calculable option fails because a requirement that changes cannot be calculated, which is the definition of the varying schedule. The both-equally option fails because the average conceals the very thing that determines the response, namely how likely the next click is to pay.

questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: Building a Behaviour Step by Step
questions.learningObjective: define shaping in terms of successive approximations
questions.stem: A pigeon is first reinforced for turning towards a key, then for touching it, then for pressing it, and within an hour presses it with no prompting. What is this procedure?

Extinction, in which reinforcement is withdrawn until the behaviour appears without any help
options.misconception: reverses the giving of reinforcement and the taking of it away

options.text: Chaining, in which a whole sequence is learnt before any part of it is ever reinforced
options.misconception: confuses building a chain of cues with reinforcing successive approximations

options.text: Classical conditioning, in which the key becomes a signal for food on its own without pressing
options.misconception: uses the conditioning term for a procedure built on a behaviour's consequences

The chaining option fails because chaining refers to the order in which cues set off component responses in a sequence, and nothing here is about cues triggering each other. The classical-conditioning option fails because the key is not being turned into a signal by pairing, and the bird is acting on the world rather than reacting to a paired sound.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: How Long the Food Takes to Arrive
questions.learningObjective: state the effect of delaying reinforcement on response strength
questions.stem: In one condition a rat's lever press is followed by food immediately, and in a second the same food arrives ten seconds later. What is the delay doing?

options.text: Lengthening it weakens the press-to-food contingency, so the delayed condition yields a lower press rate
Lengthening it sharpens the contingency, so the delayed condition yields a higher press rate
options.misconception: assumes a longer gap makes a consequence easier to link to the act

options.text: It changes nothing, since the amount of food delivered is identical in the two conditions
options.misconception: believes only the size of a consequence can matter to learning

options.text: It turns the second condition into extinction, since food there no longer follows the press
options.misconception: treats a weaker contingency as the absence of any contingency

questions.explanation: A consequence teaches a behaviour to the extent that the behaviour can be used to work out when it will arrive, and an immediate payoff makes the connection tight while a ten-second gap lets other events slip in between, so the press becomes a weaker predictor and the rate falls accordingly. This is why delivery machines that confirm a choice at once build the habit fastest, and why a trainer who praises long after the act is training something less precise. The sharper option fails because it reverses the reasoning about predictability, and a longer wait can only make the link to the act harder to use. The nothing option fails because amount and timing are separate properties of a contingency, and a great deal of learning research concerns timing alone. The extinction option fails because food still arrives, so there is a contingency to be weakened, and extinction is its absence rather than its dilution.
questions.hint: Ask how well the press predicts the food in each condition, and what that is worth.

questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: Why the Unreliable Machine Keeps Someone Playing
questions.learningObjective: explain resistance to extinction under partial reinforcement
questions.stem: A machine pays out on about one pull in five, and a player stays for hours, while a machine that pays every pull is abandoned after an hour. What explains the longer persistence?

options.text: Partial reinforcement, since long stretches go unrewarded, so each next pull could still be the one that pays
Continuous reinforcement, since a guaranteed payoff makes a player want the habit to continue
options.misconception: credits the schedule that extinguishes fastest with resisting extinction

options.text: Extinction, since the unrewarded pulls are teaching the player that the machine is worthless
options.misconception: uses the name for a loss of responding to explain a resistance to it

options.text: Shaping, since the hours at the machine train a sequence of approaches to the handle
options.misconception: reads a long run of persistence as a deliberately built response chain

The praise need not have been anything the cook found rewarding in itself, because reinforcement is defined by its effect on the act rather than by its size or its warmth, and a person praised specifically and repeatedly for a dish is being told what to make. The word reward names the payoff inside the consequence, so on this occasion the payoff may be nothing beyond the owner's approval, and keeping the two apart lets you ask the sharper question of whether the cook would still have served the dish had nobody praised it. A consequence the cook found satisfying and a consequence the owner found satisfying are different things, and it is the cook's reaction that determines whether the behaviour rises. The pattern described, an act that repeats and a standard that stops improving, is what a consequence acting on the wrong target looks like, and the remedy follows directly from the analysis rather than from a general plea for better criticism. Praise that names the next improvement would put the consequence on the behaviour that needs to change. A test the analysis suggests is a kitchen where the owner praises a different aspect each week, covering plating, seasoning and sauce, since a cook who keeps improving has been reinforced on a variable set of dimensions rather than on one fixed dish.

On the machine that pays every time the rule is that a reward is due after a small fixed number of purchases, so four failures in a row is direct evidence that something has changed, and continuing is throwing money away. Stopping is then the response to genuine information, which is why that behaviour ends quickly. On the machine that pays on about a fifth of purchases, four failures in a row is unremarkable, because the account itself says stretches like that are normal, and the player's own record cannot distinguish an unlucky patch from the start of a bad patch. Stopping is only correct if the machine is finished, and the player never has the evidence that would justify it, so the behaviour survives long past the point at which the other machine has been abandoned. The account is partial reinforcement, and the useful corollary is a counterintuitive one worth stating plainly: the schedule that teaches a behaviour fastest is the one that makes it most fragile, so guarantees are a poor way to build something you want to last. The evidence that would support the explanation is a test in which both machines are run for matched periods and then stopped paying entirely, since a schedule whose learning depended on occasional reward should be the one whose behaviour persists longest under extinction, and a schedule that paid every time should collapse almost at once.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: An Account of Giving Up Without Trying
questions.learningObjective: explain learned helplessness and specify the evidence that would separate it from rival readings
questions.stem: A student who has failed at the same puzzle every day for a month now opens it, looks at it and closes it again. Explain what an account of learned helplessness claims, and say what evidence would show the cause lies elsewhere.

answer.exemplar: The account has to start from the shape of the behaviour rather than from the feeling, and the shape is the striking part: the student has stopped attempting rather than attempting and failing, and a month in which effort demonstrably changed nothing supplies exactly the history the account needs. Its central claim is that what has been learnt is a general expectation that effort does not alter the outcome, and the reason that claim is worth testing is the prediction it makes rather than the label it attaches, because the prediction is that the withdrawal will be indiscriminate and will carry over to puzzles that are plainly within reach. A student who declines to open an easy puzzle is evidence for the account in a way that a student who tries, fails and stops is not. The rival explanations must be set out rather than waved away, since a month of failure on one task is also consistent with the task being beyond the student's current reach, with the task having become reliably tied to being seen to fail, and with the student's goals having changed so the puzzle no longer matters. Nothing in the description settles between them, and a confident answer that picks one without addressing the others has not met the standard of the question. The evidence that would separate them is a design that varies whether effort can work, giving the same student trials at a difficulty they can reach, because helplessness predicts the withdrawal follows the student there while a task-appropriateness account predicts the effort returns there and only there. What would weaken the helplessness reading is the student attempting a solvable version unprompted, because that is precisely the discrimination the account denies, and it is also the observation a teacher can make cheaply before invoking anything theoretical.

questions.explanation: The answer has to state the account's central claim as a general expectation about effort, set out at least two rival explanations, and specify a design in which the accounts predict different behaviour on an easy task.
questions.hint: Ask whether the student declines to try or tries and gives up, and whether the giving up spreads to easy tasks.

questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: Paying for Something Enjoyed Unpaid
questions.learningObjective: explain a proposed overjustification effect and the controls it needs
questions.stem: A child who sorted buttons for weeks with no payment is then paid a small sum per hundred, and soon stops sorting when the payments stop. Explain how a reward could reduce the activity, and say what a design must add.

answer.exemplar: The thing to explain is a fall in an activity that nobody has stopped paying for, so the paying must have altered something other than the amount of sorting, and the account on offer is that the activity has come to be done for the payment rather than for its own sake. Once money is attached to it, button sorting joins the category of paid work: it is done to be counted, the parts of the activity that were never going to be paid for stop being worth doing, and an interest built up over weeks of unpaid play is dismantled by an arrangement that made the interesting part the expensive part. The account is a proposal and not a settled result, and saying so is part of answering rather than a hedge, because studies reporting this effect differ in what participants were told about the study's purpose and in how the interest was measured. Three things have to be added to a design before the reading is supported. A no-payment group has to be run identically and followed for as long, since interest in any novel activity falls over time regardless of money, and a falling control group turns the finding into evidence about time rather than about payment. The measure of interest has to be independent of the paid behaviour, or the fall in interest and the fall in paid sorting are the same number wearing two names. And a condition has to vary the contingency, paying by time at the table rather than by buttons sorted, which tests whether it is the presence of money or the counting that does the work. What would argue against the account is interest that returns promptly once the payments stop, since a diversion is a weaker claim than a lost appetite, and what would support it is interest that does not come back.

questions.explanation: The answer has to give a mechanism in which the payment changes the reason for the activity, concede that the finding is a proposal under dispute, and specify the control group, the independent measure and the contingency variation the design needs.
questions.hint: Ask what the sorting is now done for, and what a no-payment group and an independent measure of interest would add.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: Claims About Reinforcement and Punishment
questions.learningObjective: evaluate claims about what counts as reinforcement and what makes punishment work
questions.stem: Four claims about reinforcement and punishment are offered. Which two of them are supported? Select both.

options.text: A consequence counts as reinforcement only if the behaviour becomes more likely after it arrives
Punishment is likelier to work when its consequence lands at the moment of the behaviour
Removing a valued toy after a tantrum counts as positive rather than negative punishment
options.misconception: labels a removal by how it feels rather than by what happened

options.text: Any act by an authority after a misbehaviour counts as punishment for that misbehaviour
options.misconception: treats any action after a misbehaviour as a punishment whatever its effect

questions.explanation: The first of the supported pair is close to a definition, and stating it precisely is worth the trouble because most of the confusion in this area comes from looser versions of it. Reinforcement is named by what the consequence did to the behaviour rather than by how pleasant the consequence was, so a consequence that is followed by the same behaviour is not a reinforcer however much the recipient enjoyed it. The second supported claim is about timing and it is a claim about effectiveness rather than about naming, since a consequence that lands in the same moment as the act can attach to that act, while one that arrives much later attaches to whatever happens in between. The positive-and-negative option fails because the pair of words describes what was done to a stimulus, with positive meaning added and negative meaning removed, and the toy was removed rather than added, so it is the negative kind. The any-act option fails because naming an action punishment is a claim about its effect, and an authority's glare that leaves the misbehaviour exactly as frequent was not punishment at all.
questions.hint: Ask what a consequence has to do to the behaviour to earn the name, and when it has to arrive.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: Claims About Schedules of Reinforcement
questions.learningObjective: evaluate claims about the response patterns different schedules produce
questions.stem: Four claims about schedules of reinforcement are offered. Which two of them are supported? Select both.

options.text: A fixed-ratio schedule tends to produce a pause after each reward and then a high steady rate
A variable-interval schedule tends to produce a steady moderate rate with no pauses at all
A fixed-interval schedule pays out the same number of responses as a variable-ratio one
options.misconception: confuses a pay rule based on elapsed time with one based on a count

options.text: A variable-ratio schedule produces a slow rate, since a reward that cannot be predicted is worth less
options.misconception: assumes an unpredictable reward removes the value of trying at all

questions.explanation: The first supported claim is a pattern rather than a naming claim, and it follows from what the animal knows. Under a fixed count the animal is always a known number of responses short of a reward at the moment it receives one, so it pauses through the part of the count where acting cannot pay and then works quickly through the part where it can, which produces a pause followed by a high rate. The second supported claim is the mirror image in time: under a varying interval the animal cannot know when the next reward is due, so waiting buys nothing and the steady moderate rate is what is left. The same-count option fails because the two schedules are defined by different things altogether, one by elapsed time and the other by a number of responses, so there is no sense in which they deliver the same number of responses per reward. The slow-rate option fails because the variable-ratio schedule is the one most resistant to extinction, and a reward that might be one response away is worth more rather than less.
questions.hint: Ask what the animal can work out in advance under each pay rule, and what waiting is worth.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: Claims About Learning by Watching
questions.learningObjective: evaluate claims about observational learning and its limits
questions.stem: Four claims about learning by watching are offered. Which two of them are supported? Select both.

options.text: A behaviour can be picked up by watching it, without the learner ever receiving its consequences
What a model is seen doing is acquired more readily than what the model is heard recommending
A single viewing of a complex sequence guarantees that it will be reproduced perfectly
options.misconception: claims one exposure is enough for flawless reproduction of a motor sequence

options.text: Only a live model can teach a behaviour, since a written account carries no information about it
options.misconception: rules out written and recorded models on the strength of no evidence

questions.explanation: The first supported claim commits only to a route, and it is a modest claim rather than a large one: a behaviour can be acquired without the learner having produced it and felt what follows from it, which is the whole content of learning by watching and is well established for many behaviours. The second is the more interesting of the pair, because what a model does and what a model says are demonstrably not equally effective, and the difference matters practically for anyone designing instructions. The single-viewing option fails because the two claims are easy to run together and should not be: a child can produce a bow correctly after one viewing and still get the sequence wrong in places, and a guaranteed perfect reproduction is a claim about the reliability of one exposure that no evidence supports. The live-model option fails because people learn effective sequences from diagrams, demonstrations on a screen and written descriptions, and a recorded model is still a model doing rather than recommending.
questions.hint: Ask what a route-to-learning claim commits to, and whether one exposure is the same thing as a reliable one.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: Claims About What Motivates a Person
questions.learningObjective: evaluate claims about the main accounts of motivation
questions.stem: Four claims about motivation are offered. Which two of them are supported? Select both.

options.text: An account may treat an external cue as sufficient to start an action, with no felt need involved
A set point is a value the body defends, and a departure from it is what generates a felt state
Drive reduction and incentive accounts make opposite predictions about which animals will drink
options.misconception: claims the two accounts disagree about the same simple behaviour

options.text: The need to achieve and the need to avoid failure are one motive measured two different ways
options.misconception: collapses two motives that pick opposite ends of a difficulty range

questions.explanation: The first supported claim is about the scope of an account rather than its truth, and it is worth being precise about the distinction. An incentive account is permitted to treat a sight or a smell as sufficient to start an action, and whether that suffices in a given case is a separate question from whether the account is entitled to make the move, which is the distinction that lets the two families of accounts be treated as genuine rivals rather than as one of them being a mistake. The second supported claim sorts out two words that are routinely swapped. A set point is a value the system defends and a departure from it is an event, so the event can be what produces the felt state while the value is what the system is aiming back towards. The opposite-predictions option fails because animals drink in both accounts, and the accounts differ in what they treat as the initiating condition rather than in whether drinking happens. The one-motive option fails because the two achievement motives select opposite ends of the same difficulty range, which is what makes them distinguishable at all.
questions.hint: Ask whether the claim is about an account's scope or about which of two accounts is right, and what a set point actually is.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: The Order in Which an Association Is Built
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps by which a conditioned association is acquired
questions.stem: Put these five events in the order in which an association between a neutral sound and food is acquired.

options.text: A neutral sound is presented and produces no response of its own worth reporting
A stimulus that produces its response without any history is presented on its own
The two are presented together repeatedly, with the sound arriving before the food
The sound begins to produce its own response before the food has arrived at all
The sound is finally presented alone, with nothing following, to see whether it holds up

questions.explanation: The sequence opens with the two things that are about to be paired, each in the state it is in before the learning starts: the sound does nothing and the food already produces its response. Pairing them repeatedly is the third step, and the order within each pairing matters because the sound has to arrive early enough to be a usable warning rather than a consequence of the food. The fourth step is the evidence that the learning has happened, and its significance is that the response now precedes the food instead of following it, which is the difference between reacting to food and anticipating it. The fifth step is a test rather than a further stage of learning, and it is the one most often left out of a retelling of the procedure. The order that places the paired presentations before the two baseline events fails because nothing can be paired until both members of the pair exist and are known to behave as described. The order that puts the solo test before the response has appeared fails because the test is only interpretable once there is a learned response to test.
questions.hint: Establish what each of the two stimuli does before they meet, then pair them, then check the sound alone.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: The Order in Which a Behaviour Is Shaped
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps by which an operant behaviour is shaped
questions.stem: Put these five events in the order that leads from an organism that never performs the target act to one that performs it reliably.

options.text: The organism does something roughly in the direction of the act while the act itself never appears
That near miss is reinforced, and it becomes more frequent than it was before
The requirement is tightened so that a slightly better approximation is now the one that pays
Each version in turn is reinforced until the target act itself begins to appear
Reinforcement is thinned out, and the act continues without the reward at every occurrence

questions.explanation: The chain has to begin with something that is not the target act, because there is nothing to reinforce until the organism does something at all, and the first step is what the experimenter chooses to pay for. Reinforcing that near miss is what makes the second step possible, and the pay-off is a loop rather than a single move: each reinforcement makes the behaviour it followed more common, which gives more occasions to reinforce the next approximation. Tightening the requirement is the third step and the one that makes the procedure a procedure, since without it the organism would stay on the version that is already being paid for. The fourth step is where the target act finally appears, and the fifth is the handover from earning to performing, since a behaviour that still needs the reward on every occasion has not yet been trained. The order that places the thinning of reinforcement before the target act fails because there is nothing yet to make occasional, and the order that reinforces the near miss after tightening the requirement inverts the two operations that have to be repeated in sequence.
questions.hint: Start with the first behaviour worth paying for, reward it, then ask what has to happen for the target act ever to appear.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: The Order From Enjoyment to Abandonment
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps of a proposed overjustification sequence
questions.stem: Put these five events in the order in which a reward is said to change the reason a person does an activity.

options.text: The person does the activity week after week and is paid nothing for doing it
The activity comes to be valued for itself and the habit of doing it grows stronger
A reward arrives that is given only when a set amount of the activity has been done
The activity is now largely done for the reward, and the unpaid part of it shrinks away
The reward stops, and the activity that was once worth doing unpaid no longer draws the person

questions.explanation: The account needs the unpaid habit to exist first, because a payment cannot displace a reason for acting that was never there, and the second step is what supplies the reason the payment is later said to crowd out. The third step is where the reason changes, and the crucial detail is that the reward is contingent on a measurable amount of the activity, since a payment for mere attendance does not do the same work. The fourth step is the displacement, and it is a gradual shrinking rather than a single moment: the parts of the activity that never earn anything stop being done, and the activity comes to be done only in the part that does. The fifth step is the part that distinguishes this account from a simple loss of habit, because the interest that was built up is not restored when the payment stops. The order that places the reward before the unpaid habit fails because the crowding-out claim has nothing to crowd out at that point. The order that puts the shrinking before the payment arrives fails because the reason for the activity has not yet been moved to the payment when the shrinking is said to happen.
questions.hint: The interest has to exist before the payment can replace it, and the replacement has to precede the loss of interest.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: Pellets Earned in a Fixed-Ratio Session
questions.learningObjective: compute rewards earned under a fixed ratio from a response rate
questions.stem: On a fixed-ratio schedule a pigeon needs 20 pecks for each food pellet and pecks at one and a half a second. How many pellets does it earn in two minutes?
questions.explanation: Two minutes is 120 seconds, and at one and a half pecks a second that is 1.5 multiplied by 120, which is 180 pecks. A pellet is paid for every complete set of 20, so 180 divided by 20 gives 9 pellets. The reason the division is worth doing exactly rather than estimating is that a fixed-ratio schedule pays on completed sets only, so a session that ends part-way through a set pays nothing for that part, and rounding the number of pellets up would credit the pigeon with a reward it never received.
questions.hint: Convert the two minutes to seconds, multiply by the peck rate, then divide by the pecks a pellet costs.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: Percentage Fall in a Response Count
questions.learningObjective: express a fall between two counts as a percentage of the earlier one
questions.stem: A pigeon makes 180 pecks in the first minute of an operant session and 45 in the tenth minute. By what percentage is the tenth-minute count lower than the first?
questions.explanation: A percentage fall is measured against the earlier figure, so the drop of 180 minus 45, which is 135, is divided by the 180 to give 0.75, or 75 percent. The base matters and is the step that is easy to get wrong, because dividing the drop by the later figure of 45 would give 300 percent, which describes something far larger than what happened. Reading this as a fall in responding over a session is the reason to compute it, since a decline of this size within a single session is the pattern associated with the behaviour wearing out rather than with a change in what the schedule pays.
questions.hint: Subtract the later count from the earlier one, then divide the difference by the earlier count.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Learning and Motivation: Responses Made in a Long Session
questions.learningObjective: convert a session length in minutes into a response count at a stated rate
questions.stem: A pigeon on a varying-interval schedule responds at one peck a second, and a pellet arrives on average every three minutes. How many responses does it make in a thirty-minute session?
questions.explanation: Thirty minutes is 1800 seconds, and at one peck a second that is 1800 responses. The same session would pay out ten pellets, since 30 divided by 3 is 10, and the contrast between the two figures is the point of the exercise: the responding is steady and abundant while the payoffs are rare, which is what a schedule with an unpredictable next reward is supposed to produce, because waiting buys the animal nothing at all. A rate of one peck a second sustained for half an hour is high, and the number is worth computing rather than appreciating, since sessions of that length are where a schedule's effect on endurance is actually visible.
questions.hint: Convert the thirty minutes to seconds and multiply by the rate of one response a second.
